title: Asynchronous parameter swap and kernel affinity proposal
content:
Summary:

This proposal describes an asynchronous parameter swap mechanism combined with a kernel-affinity mapping layer to improve cold-start latency, minimize IO stalls, and allow safe hot-patching of parameter shards (including safetensors-backed artifacts) in the serving runtime. It targets scenarios where model residency cannot be guaranteed for all parameters (multi-model hosts, memory-constrained Dedicated nodes) and where kernels have differing memory/copy characteristics that we can exploit to reduce end-to-end latency.

Goals:
- Allow incremental and non-blocking replacement of parameter shards while in-use by inference workers.
- Expose kernel affinity hints so that the weight loader can prioritize placing shards in memory regions optimal for downstream kernels (e.g., pinned memory for DMA-friendly kernels, GPU-resident pages for fused-kernel paths).
- Maintain KV cache correctness and coherency during partial swaps and evictions.
- Provide safety for mmap-backed safetensors files: checksums, quarantine, and atomic rename/activation semantics to avoid torn reads.
- Provide observability and metrics to detect regressions (latency spikes, invalid outputs).

Design overview:
The design separates concerns into three cooperating components: Swap Coordinator, Loader Agents, and Kernel Affinity Mapper. These components interact with existing residency controller and KV cache modules but present a minimal-change integration surface to inference kernels.

1) Swap Coordinator (SC)
- Centralized per-node agent that serializes activation commits for parameter shards.
- Maintains a per-shard state machine: NOT_PRESENT -> LOADING -> STAGED -> ACTIVATING -> ACTIVE -> EVICTING -> REMOVED.
- Provides a two-phase commit API for activation: stage(paths, checksum) -> verify_stage(shard_id) -> commit(shard_id) -> activation_complete.
- Staging creates a quarantined mmap or temporary allocation that is visible to the SC but invisible to inference workers until commit.
- Commit atomically swaps the shard pointer in the residency map; workers switch to the new backing via an epoch-based read handle described below.

2) Loader Agents
- Responsible for fetching shards from remote object store or local cache, performing any necessary conversion (safetensors unpacking, quantization on-the-fly), and placing them into the appropriate memory region.
- Loader chooses allocation strategy guided by Kernel Affinity Mapper: pinned host memory, GPU direct copy buffer, numa-local pinned region, or mmap.
- Loader computes a SHA256 checksum and expected size; attaches metadata (format, dtype, quantization profile) to the staged shard.
- On failure, Loader cleans up staged allocations and reports error codes to SC; does not corrupt existing residency map.

3) Kernel Affinity Mapper (KAM)
- Small policy engine that maps shard characteristics and kernel signatures to preferred placement. For example:
  - Large dense attention weights used by fused CUDA kernels -> GPU-resident pages preferred.
  - Small projection matrices used by tiny kernels -> pinned host memory with CPU-side prefetch.
  - KV-cache keys -> host-proximal heap region with eviction hooks linked to KV LRU.
- KAM exposes an API: suggest_placement(shard_metadata, kernel_profile) -> [placement_hint, priority_score].
- Priority influences Loader ordering under IO contention.

Worker integration and epoch handles:
- Workers access parameter shards through an indirection: a shard handle map that references a small structure {version, pointer, placement_hint}. Reads from the map are performed under an epoch-snapshot: worker starts inference epoch, pins the current shard pointers, and uses them for the duration of the request.
- Activation commits bump the shard version and atomically swap the pointer. Ongoing requests continue using their epoch snapshot until completion; new requests see the new shard.
- This avoids stop-the-world copy-on-write. The residency controller still enforces soft memory limits and coordinates eviction only for shards not referenced by active epochs.

KV cache coherence:
- KV cache entries reference parameter shard versions. When a shard is activated, SC emits an event so KV cache can validate entries produced by older versions. Basic strategies:
  1) Conservative: invalidate all KV entries that depend on a replaced shard. Simple but can increase cache misses during heavy rollouts.
  2) Versioned keys: tag KV entries with parameter version id; lookups first match current version id, otherwise fall back to recompute.
- Default: use versioned keys for critical KV regions (attention caches) and conservative invalidation as a fallback for rarely-updated components.

Memory and mmap safety for safetensors and on-disk artifacts:
- All incoming safetensors blobs are verified (format and SHA256) before staging. If the file is stored on local disk, it is opened read-only and mapped into a quarantined address space that prevents execution or writes.
- Staging path uses a temporary filename in the same filesystem to guarantee atomic rename semantics during activation. The sequence is:
  1) write blob to tmp-file.
  2) fsync(tmp-file) to ensure durability.
  3) compute checksum.
  4) rename(tmp-file -> final-file)  // atomic on POSIX; avoids torn-reader scenarios for readers opening final-file after rename.
- For memory-mapped loading, the Loader performs mmap on tmp-file and maps it into a private anonymous region if on-the-fly conversion is required. The SC only switches the runtime pointer to this mapped region after commit.
- If host page faults occur during activation, the SC can abort commit and leave previous pointer intact; abort path includes draining any partial references and releasing mmap.

Eviction policy and IO backpressure shaping:
- Residency controller will call SC to request eviction candidates. SC will consider: active epochs count, kernel affinity priority, last-access timestamp, and size.
- Eviction of a shard in ACTIVATING or LOADING is prohibited; delete requests are transformed into delayed evictions to avoid race-induced crashes.
- IO shaping: under high outgoing load to object store, Loader reduces parallelism and reorders according to kernel-affinity priority_score. Lower-priority loads may be throttled or cancelled to preserve latency SLOs for high-priority kernels.

Hot swap and rollback semantics:
- Commits are idempotent operations that advance version. If a post-commit health check (see observability) fails on a small % of traffic, SC supports automatic rollback to the previous version within a configurable rollback-window (default 5 minutes). Rollback is implemented by another atomic pointer swap.
- Rollback must preserve safety semantics: no active epoch should be forced to use a rolled-back pointer. Instead, new epochs see the rolled-back pointer; existing epochs continue with whatever they pinned.

Observability and health checks:
- SC emits the following metrics per-shard: load_time_ms, stage_failures, commit_latency_ms, active_epochs, current_version, last_eviction_time, io_retries.
- Health check flow for commits: run a short canary trace (synthetic inference path) on a configurable sampling rate (default 0.5% traffic). If synthetic outputs diverge from expected ranges or latency > threshold, mark the commit as degraded and trigger rollback policy.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for state transitions in SC, including all error and abort paths.
- Integration tests that simulate concurrent requests pinned to older epochs while new versions are committed and evicted.
- Chaos tests: simulate partial disk corruption, aborted downloads, and delayed fsync to ensure no torn reads or crashes.
- Performance tests: measure cold-start with prioritized kernel-affinity placement vs baseline full-mmap.

API and config knobs (suggested):
- runtime.loader.parallel_fetch_limit: int
- runtime.swap.commit_timeout_ms: int
- runtime.swap.rollback_window_ms: int
- runtime.kam.priority_weights: json-stringified map (kernel_type -> weight)
- runtime.swap.health_check_sample_rate: float

Backward compatibility and migration path:
- New SC and Loader are opt-in via node config. Existing residency map remains compatible; Loader exposes a compatibility shim to load legacy file layouts.
- Gradual rollout: start with non-critical model families, ramp to all models after 2 weeks of stability.

Security considerations:
- Ensure staged artifacts are written with correct owner and mode bits; temporary files must be created with O_EXCL and secure umask.
- Checksums must be validated and matched against signed manifests where available.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Should we allow speculative prefetch of next-version shards based on rollout schedule? (pros: faster warm start; cons: wasted IO).
- How strict should KV invalidation be for composite models with many small shards?
- Do we permit lazy conversion (quantization) on first use vs conversion during staging?

Next steps / action items:
- PR: implement minimal SC state machine and commit/abort paths (assignee: Diego).
- KAM prototype: simple rule engine and offline profiling to generate default priority_weights (assignee: Priya).
- E2E tests and chaos harness integration in CI (assignee: Evan).

Appendix: example commit trace (simplified)
1) API: request load shard S v1 -> Loader begins fetch, SC marks LOADING
2) Loader writes tmp-file, fsync, computes checksum, mmap tmp-file as quarantined region, reports STAGED to SC
3) SC verify_stage: checksum ok, run quick canary on sample input -> PASS
4) SC commit: atomically swap shard pointer, bump version to v1.1, emit commit metric
5) New worker epochs see v1.1, old epochs continue with pinned pointer until they complete
6) After grace window and active_epochs==0, eviction may remove previous backing

This spec is intentionally conservative in its safety model while enabling aggressive placement optimizations via kernel-affinity. Feedback requested on the KAM scoring design and the operational rollback window default.
